paragraphs: (b) Sotah (12a), 'She saw that he was good': R. Meir says his name was Tov; R. Yehudah says, etc.; R. Neḥemyah says, etc.; Others say he was born circumcised. Tosafot there (see also Avodah Zarah 64b) asks: since R. Meir says his name was Tov, Others must be someone other than R. Meir. Yet the end of Horayot says they designated R. Meir 'Others.' In the first chapter of Berakhot (9b), R. Meir and Others give different opinions (R. Akiva also gives an opinion); also Berakhot 47b, Sotah 22, Bava Batra 16b, Zevaḥim 46; see above, Others mentioned without R. Meir. My teacher [the Tosafist] said he saw in a French commentary that teachings received from Elisha ben Avuyah were assigned to Others because his name was Aḥer, whereas other teachings bore Meir's name. Sefer Keritot, Yemot Olam§19, writes likewise. This is unconvincing: they designated R. Natan 'Some say,' and surely assigned all his teachings thus; they did likewise for R. Meir. (Be'er Sheva, Horayot 13b, says the Elisha explanation is impossible because the name was imposed as a penalty; perhaps teachings preceding the designation retained his name. End of quotation. Yet why did he state only the few laws designated Others after that incident? This requires examination.) Rather, after they designated him Others, he retracted and said Moses was born circumcised; likewise in the first chapter of Berakhot; see Tosafot there. End of Tosafot. Be'er Sheva adds: nevertheless they did not wish to disgrace him by calling him singular 'Other'; or because others assisted him. The same explains R. Natan's plural 'Some say.' End of quotation. Responsa Ḥut HaShani says Be'er Sheva's explanation that later statements bear Others is Tosafot's at the end of Sotah's first chapter. Tosafot also mentions and rejects the Elisha explanation. End of quotation. As for Tosafot's retraction explanation, Sefer Keritot, Leshon Limmudim, gate 1§30, likewise writes: Rosh HaShanah 8 has R. Meir expound 'You shall surely tithe'; Keritot 11 has Others say the Torah speaks in human language, and Others is R. Meir. Perhaps at life's end, after the Horayot incident, he retracted that exposition. Likewise Rabbi retracted in old age concerning gold acquiring silver; Jerusalem Talmud, Kilayim 3, has R. Yishmael retract in old age (see R. Yose ben HaḤotef). Yefeh To'ar, Shemot Rabbah 1§100, asks: after he retracted, why teach his earlier words? Why not place Others immediately after R. Meir, rather than interpose R. Yoshiyah (and R. Neḥemyah and R. Akiva)? He adds: although R. Meir was designated Others, not every Others necessarily means R. Meir; sometimes an unnamed person's view requires 'Others say.' Therefore when that view accompanies R. Meir's, R. Meir must be named to distinguish them. End of quotation. But when Others appears alone, how can one know whether it is R. Meir or an unnamed person? If every lone Others is R. Meir, how throughout the Shas could an unnamed view occur only on a subject where R. Meir also states his opinion? The Holy One did not speak in R. Meir's name because he learned from Elisha Aḥer; see above, Rabbah bar Shila.

(c) His wife was Beruryah, daughter of R. Ḥanina ben Teradyon. She told R. Meir, 'It disgraces me that my sister sits in a prostitutes' booth.' He took a tarkav of dinars and went, saying, 'If no transgression has been committed with her, a miracle will occur.' Disguising himself as a horseman, he solicited her. She said she was menstruating. He offered to wait; she said there were many prettier women. He concluded no transgression had been committed with her. He gave her guard the tarkav: half to appease the king if accused, half for himself. The guard asked how to escape when the dinars were exhausted. Meir said to say, 'God of Meir, answer me.' The guard asked who could guarantee this. There were man-eating dogs; Meir threw a clod at them. They came to devour him; he said the formula, and they left him. He handed her over. The king heard and sought to hang the guard; he said the formula, and they took him down. Asked why they could not hang him, he told the story. They engraved R. Meir's likeness at Rome's gates so anyone seeing him would arrest him. One day they saw and pursued him. He ran into a brothel so they would say it could not be him, since he would not go there. Some say Elijah appeared as a prostitute and embraced him as though familiar with him. Others say there was gentile-cooked food: he dipped one finger and sucked another (see Kohelet Rabbah at 'Wisdom is good with an inheritance'). They said R. Meir would not act thus; he fled to Babylonia. Some say he fled because of Beruryah's affair. Rashi explains: she mocked the sages' statement that women are light-minded (and wrote in her book, 'except Beruryah'—Shalshelet HaKabbalah 32a [as identified in a printed witness]). He said she would ultimately acknowledge them, and ordered a student to tempt her into a transgression. He pressed her for many days until she yielded (R. Meir entered in the student's place—Shalshelet HaKabbalah [as identified in a printed witness]). When she learned what had happened she strangled herself; R. Meir fled in shame, Avodah Zarah 18. Although R. Meir belonged to the third group, he lived in the first group's time: R. Yehoshua said of a law on which Beruryah disagreed with her father, 'Beruryah has spoken well' (see her entry). See my separate page explaining that R. Meir could not have lived in R. Yehoshua's time. She learned three hundred laws from three hundred sages on a winter's day. He was alive at the marriage of R. Shimon son of Rabbi (see his entry). He married another wife, Zeruz's daughter (see R. Yehoshua ben Zeruz).

(d) He was a scribe, knowing the entire Torah by heart with its precise defective and full spellings, Eruvin 13a. R. Shimon ben Elazar says R. Meir went to Asia to intercalate years. There was no Megillah there; he wrote it from memory and read it. They said 'Your eyelids shall look straight before you' was fulfilled in him, Megillah 18b. Jerusalem Talmud, Megillah 4, halakhah 1, says he wrote a second copy from the written first copy and read from the second. Gittin 67a calls him sage and scribe; Rashi refers to Sotah 20, 'I told him: I am a scribe.' Midrash Kohelet: R. Meir was an excellent scribe, earning three sela each week: one for food and drink, one for clothing, one to support the rabbis. Eruvin there: the Holy One knows none in his generation equaled him, yet the law was not fixed according to him because his colleagues could not fathom his reasoning: he would call pure impure and impure pure and demonstrate arguments. Sanhedrin 24: seeing R. Meir in the study house was like seeing mountains uprooted and ground together. There 38b, he expounded one-third halakhah, one-third aggadah, one-third parables; he had three hundred fox parables. Mishnah, Eglah Arufah 49: when R. Meir died, parable-makers ceased. Rabbi—some read Rav—said his greater sharpness came from seeing R. Meir from behind (see Abba Arikha and R. Yehudah HaNasi). Jerusalem Talmud, beginning of Nedarim 9: whoever held R. Meir's staff learned wisdom from it; see the commentary's other interpretation, and R. Shimon ben Elazar, who served him and held his staff. Jerusalem Talmud, HaYah Kore, mishnah 7, and Mo'ed Katan 3, halakhah 5: his colleague R. Yose praised him to Tzippori's people as great, holy and modest. Once he greeted mourners on Shabbat, etc. Gittin 52a: two people quarreled every Sabbath eve; R. Meir came and restrained them for three Sabbath eves until they made peace. Satan said, 'Woe, R. Meir has expelled that man from his house.' Yoma 83b: he scrutinized names. At an inn whose host was Kidor, he said he was wicked, from 'For they are a perverse generation.' On Friday he hid his purse in the cemetery at the host's father's grave. The father told his son in a dream to take the purse at his head. Next day the host told R. Meir; he answered that Sabbath-eve dreams are futile, and recovered his purse that evening. Why not say dreams have no effect, as Meir himself said—see Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel of Yavneh? Perhaps he feared disbelief and a search at the grave, so he specified Sabbath-eve dreams: the host would wait for another dream on a weekday night, and R. Meir would meanwhile retrieve it after Shabbat. He mocked transgressors. One day Satan appeared as a woman across the river. There was no ferry; Meir seized the rope and crossed. Halfway, the evil impulse left him, saying: but for the heavenly proclamation to beware of R. Meir and his Torah, I would have made your blood worth two ma'ah, Asarah Yuḥasin 81a. He said, 'Guard me against my daughter,' there. Tosefta Shabbat 12 and the chapter “Rabbi Eliezer of circumcision” 134a: when ill, his student R. Shimon ben Elazar undertook to prepare a remedy, but Meir would not let him, saying that though he permitted others, he had never brought himself to transgress his colleagues' words. So too Jerusalem Talmud, Berakhot 1, mishnah 2. In his days they found a dove image among the Samaritans on Mount Gerizim, first chapter of Ḥullin. They had been accepted in Shimon the Righteous's days, but in R. Meir's returned to their misconduct and were disqualified (see above, part 1, year 3448; Ritva; Me'or Einayim 21). Queen Cleopatra questioned R. Meir, Sanhedrin 90b. A woman heard his exposition; her scoffing husband told her to spit in R. Meir's face (see Bava ben Buta). See at length R. Yehudah of Anatot, whom R. Meir saved from death.

(e) R. Akiva said: 'I traveled by ship and saw another ship battered at sea. I grieved for the Torah scholar aboard—R. Meir. On reaching Cappadocia he sat and discussed law before me. I asked, "My son, who brought you up?" He said, "One wave drove me to another until it cast me ashore." I then said: How great are the sages' words that the wife of one lost in waters without a visible limit remains prohibited,' Yevamot 121a. All this also happened to R. Akiva (see his entry). Wherever a student speaks in R. Yishmael's name before R. Akiva, it is R. Meir. He first learned from R. Akiva, then R. Yishmael, then R. Akiva (see his entry). He was R. Akiva's principal student; R. Akiva appointed him and he sat at the head, while R. Shimon's face changed (see his entry). R. Akiva ordained him but they did not accept him because he was young; afterward R. Yehudah ben Bava ordained him, Sanhedrin 14a. He died outside the Land, in Asia, directing that his coffin be placed on the seashore, Jerusalem Talmud, end of Kilayim. South of Tiberias, toward the hot springs, is the grave of R. Meir, Elisha's student (גא״י [provisionally Gelilot Eretz Yisrael]). He died before R. Yehudah and R. Yose, as in Kiddushin 2(52); see R. Yehudah HaNasi and Sumkhos.

(f) R. Meir descended from Nero, whom the emperor sent to destroy the Temple. Nero asked a child for his verse; he recited, 'I shall place My vengeance upon Edom by My people Israel's hand.' Nero said the Holy One wanted to wipe His hands on him; he fled and converted, and R. Meir descended from him, Gittin 56a; see part 1, year 3829. Gilgulei Neshamot (Nun 4) says Nero was repaired in R. Meir; Nero was Samlah of Masrekah, for all hearing his cruelty hissed, and this was his repair. Yalkut Reuveni, Bereshit 27b, cites kabbalists: R. Meir was a spark of Metatron. Megalleh Amukot, ofan 252, says the small alef of Vayikra is Metatron, Prince of the Presence, numerically elef, one thousand, less one, in the mystery of 'one interceding angel out of a thousand.' Therefore R. Meir's Torah, since his nourishment and wisdom came from alef through Metatron's spark, read 'garments of light' with alef. Metatron held the tree of knowledge of good and evil—Metatron and ס״ס [Samael, provisional]. Thus the initial letters of מיץ אפים יוציא ריב form Meir; the final letters total 133, the value of בסמאל, 'I hate in Samael'; אפים has Samael's value. He contains good and evil because he descended from converted Nero. Yalkut Reuveni says the initials of המון גוים נתתיך form Nogah, for converts come from the shell of Nogah. Kohelet Shelomoh 12 says this shell is called red heifer, for it purifies the impure when good prevails, and sometimes the reverse, etc. This is what I found in the writings of my father and teacher: wise words, worthy of a kiss. (It says plural 'angers,' not singular anger, because he was a spark of Metatron holding good and evil: good from Metatron, evil from Samael; forty-nine aspects of purity against good and forty-nine of impurity against evil. Thus they could not fathom R. Meir's thought, for he could purify a creeping creature by forty-nine arguments and give forty-nine arguments for impurity. Therefore he needed to learn from Aḥer, who held the tree of knowledge of good and evil. Hence 'R. Meir found a pomegranate': the interior of מטטרון is טט, the mystery of nine vowel points of letters and nine Torah accents; removing these leaves רמון, pomegranate. He held those letters and ate its interior, the two tets, but threw away its shell. End of Yalkut Reuveni quotation.)

(g) The law follows R. Meir in his decrees, Ketubbot 57a, 60b, but not his penalties, Tosafot Yevamot 37a, 'Does he act.' Also Tosafot Zevaḥim 104a citing Halakhot Gedolot; Bava Kamma 30b, 'And the sages say'; chapter Eizehu Neshekh 72a, 78a, 'To render impure.' See Bava Batra 94b; Beitzah 27a, 'Rather, R. Meir'; Bekhorot 28a; Eruvin 47a. Responsa Ḥavvot Yair cites Eruvin as excluding the view that the law follows R. Meir in his decrees. We hold like R. Meir in decrees even against R. Yose (see his entry, where I wrote the opposite; this requires examination, since the book is not now before me), all the more against R. Shimon. See Tosafot Yom Tov, end of Nedarim 2, and Tosafot 20b: why not rule like R. Meir because his decrees are his stringencies? Perhaps this rule is reckoned only regarding his penalties. End of quotation. See Tosafot Yom Tov, Avodah Zarah 1:5: what he writes is unconvincing, since everyone there decrees where a decree is appropriate. In my humble opinion the Shas proves we follow R. Meir, since it objects to him about a fine palm tree, etc. Why object to R. Meir by inference, rather than to the first tanna and R. Yehudah, who permit even a fine palm? Necessarily it adopts R. Meir's view; see there. We follow R. Meir's decrees even against the majority, as Ketubbot 57a proves. Tosafot Shabbat 9a, 'A decree,' and 11b, 'He shall not stand.' In Kol Gaggot, here we do not follow R. Meir. See Oraḥ Mishor, Nazir, novellae on Maimonides: Maimonides 2, law 19, says a slave who vowed naziriteship and fled may not drink wine, so he suffers and returns to his master. The source then reads ובריבית [difficult fragment]; in the glosses, Raavad says the law follows R. Yose, who permits drinking. See Tosafot Yom Tov. In my opinion Maimonides follows R. Meir's decrees, meaning his stringencies, as Eruvin 47a and Ketubbot 57a: here too he is stringent so the slave suffers and returns. Though Rashi calls it penalizing the slave, and the law does not follow R. Meir's penalties, 'penalty' is not precise here; it means imposing a stringency. Maimonides' code, Mishnah commentary and Bartenura do not use 'penalty.' That term properly applies to interest, Bava Kamma 30b, Bava Metzia 72, Bava Batra 94; here one should say stringency. Moreover, according to Tosafot Yom Tov, end of Nedarim 2, Tosafot is unsure whether the law follows R. Meir even in penalties; perhaps Maimonides does rule like him in penalties. Though R. Meir disagrees with R. Yehudah in a baraita, the law follows R. Meir because most anonymous Mishnah follows him: Eruvin 96, Gittin 4, Sanhedrin 86. This despite the rule favoring R. Yehudah against R. Meir, as Alfasi, Kol HaKelim, writes against Halakhot Gedolot. Tosafot Beitzah 2b explains that anonymity counts as a majority. Here R. Meir's view is anonymous and thus the majority, R. Yose the individual; the law follows the majority. See Oraḥ Mishor.

(e [source repeats this letter]) A story of R. Meir, who went up to Jerusalem each festival and lodged with Yehudah the butcher. His beautiful, modest wife was diligent in honoring R. Meir. She died; Yehudah remarried and told his new wife to honor the scholar R. Meir if he came. At the festival R. Meir arrived and asked after the first wife. Told she had died, he wept and wished to leave. The new wife seized his garment, saying her husband had instructed her to honor him even more than the first. R. Meir said he could not enter without the husband's permission. Outside he met and greeted R. Yehudah, who told him his wife had died but the new one was more diligent in honoring him. R. Meir entered; she brought food and drink and served him. He was young and very handsome. She desired him and intoxicated him until he could not distinguish right from left. She spread a bed; he lay down, and she lay with him until morning. In his drunkenness he was unaware of her lying down or rising. The narrator says that he dallied with her all night. Next morning he went to the study house to pray. On returning she again brought food and drink and talked and joked with him. He wondered at her boldness, looked down and would not gaze at her. She asked why: he had played with her all night, yet was now ashamed. He said, 'Heaven forbid; nothing of the sort occurred.' She identified a mark on his body as proof. He realized he had acted madly with her, grieved bitterly, wept and cried: 'Woe, I have lost the Torah I learned! What remedy have I?' He resolved to confess to the academy head and accept whatever he imposed. Returning home, he cried throughout the journey with torn clothes and ashes on his head. His relatives asked what happened; he told them. Asked his intention, he said he would go to the academy head and accept his commands. They said it was inadvertent and God would forgive; he should keep quiet lest he bring disgrace upon his children. He answered that listening to them would prevent forgiveness, for 'One who conceals his transgressions will not prosper.' He went to the academy head. Asked his wish, he said, 'Light of the world, this happened; I shall accept whatever you say, death or life or being fed to lions.' The sage told him to wait while he examined his case. Next day he ruled that he be fed to lions. R. Meir accepted Heaven's judgment. The sage summoned two strong Israelites to take him to a forest of lions, bind his hands and feet, leave him, and watch from trees. If eaten, they should bring his bones for lamentation because he accepted Heaven's judgment. At midnight a lion came, smelled him and left. They reported; the sage directed a second night. A lion roared, smelled him and left. He ordered a third night; if untouched, they should return him, since no heavenly judgment lay upon him. At midnight a lion roared, struck with its teeth, tore a rib from his vertebra and ate from it. They reported next day. The sage said to bring him: since it ate an olive's bulk, it was as though it ate him entirely. They brought him; he ordered physicians to heal him. When R. Meir returned home, a heavenly voice declared him destined and prepared for life in the world to come. End of quotation, from an unidentified small book.

(i) R. Meir reports that R. Eliezer says (Yoma 59a). R. Eliezer ben Yaakov, his teacher. R. Elazar son of R. Yose, in his name, Ḥullin 38. R. Elazar ben Shammua, his colleague. R. Elazar said, 'We said to Meir.' R. Elazar bar Tzadok, in his name. R. Elazar ben Dolai. Elisha Aḥer, his teacher; see his entry and above. Efrayim Maksha'ah, his student. Dostai son of R. Yannai, his student. Dostai of Yishvav asked him. Rav Huna and R. Avin, in his name. Zivtai, his son-in-law, according to Yuḥasin. Zeruz, his father-in-law. R. Ḥalafta of Kefar Ḥananyah, his student; Ḥalafta, R. Yose's father, his colleague. R. Ḥanina ben Gamliel disagrees with him. R. Ḥanan, in his name. R. Ḥananyah the deputy High Priest. Ḥananyah of Ono. Ḥananyah ben Teradyon, his father-in-law. His son-in-law, in his name, Shabbat 153. R. Tarfon, his teacher. Yadua the Babylonian, his student. R. Yehudah ben Bava ordained him. R. Yehudah said, 'Meir used to say,' Ḥagigah 19a; R. Yehudah in R. Meir's name, Avodah Zarah 66. R.Y.B.B. [ריב״ב, read as R. Yehudah ben Beteira in a printed witness] debated before him. R. Yehudah ben Shammua, his student. R. Yehudah ben Agra, in his name. R. Yehoshua ben Zeruz, his father-in-law's son. R. Yehoshua ben Mammal, in his time. R. Yoḥanan the Sandalmaker, his colleague. R. Yoḥanan, in his name. R. Yose ben HaḤotef, his colleague. Abba Yose ben Yoḥanan, in his name. R. Yose ben Ḥalafta, his colleague, called him Meir. Abba Yose ben Yoḥanan of Jerusalem, in his name. The early R. Yannai, in his time. R. Yaakov, in R. Meir's name. R. Yaakov of Kefar Ḥitya, in his time. Abba Yirmeyah, in his name. R. Yishmael, his teacher (see above). R. Levi, in his name. R. Naḥman said, 'R. Meir used to say.' Nimos the weaver asked him. R. Natan, his colleague (see above). Sumkhos, his student. R. Akiva, his teacher (see above). R. Akiva ben Dosa, in his time. R. Peda said, 'R. Meir used to say.' Rav, his student. Rabbi, his student (see above). R. Shemuel Peragrito, in his name. R. Shimon, his student (see above). R. Shimon son of Rabbi (see above). R. Shimon ben Elazar, his student (see above). R. Shimon ben Yehudah of Kefar Akko, in R. Meir's name, Bereshit Rabbah 15. R. Shimon Shezuri, his colleague. R. Shimon bar Kappara. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says: R. Meir used to say, 'One who says: Give a shekel to my sons,' etc., Tosefta Ketubbot, end of chapter 6. In R. Meir's name, Bava Metzia 106b.
